feedback: For 'frequency doubles at fixed speed': the wavelength HALVES; an 'unchanged' or 'doubles' answer means the learner is not holding speed constant — restate that v is fixed, so λ = v/f must fall.
For the oscilloscope item: the correct answer is the PERIOD, because the horizontal axis is time; choosing 'wavelength' treats the time graph as a spatial picture.
For 'radio waves are sound': note that radio and light are transverse electromagnetic waves while sound is longitudinal — the types are often taught in separate lessons and wrongly merged.
If height and width are swapped on the diagram: re-anchor amplitude as vertical displacement from rest and wavelength as one full horizontal cycle.

Note on the sort: at this level water surface ripples are classified as transverse (the KS3 'transverse motion' convention); their real surface motion is more complex, which is a refinement for later study, not a reason to reclassify them here.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can annotate the canonical diagram correctly, classify wave types across domains (radio and light are transverse EM; sound is longitudinal), and apply v = fλ while tracking that speed is held fixed so frequency and wavelength trade off.
learnerActions: Label a wave diagram: amplitude (rest level to crest), wavelength (crest to crest), crest and trough — taking care not to mislabel the height as a wavelength or crest-to-trough as one wavelength.
Sort example waves — water ripples, sound, light, radio — into transverse or longitudinal, and give a reason for each.
Use v = fλ to find the missing quantity given the other two, working the calculation in both directions.
Answer: 'If frequency doubles while wave speed stays constant, what happens to the wavelength?' and justify the answer using which quantity is held constant.
Answer: 'Peak-to-peak spacing on a sound wave's oscilloscope trace is the …?' choosing between period and wavelength, and say why.
activities.title: Label, classify and calculate

feedback: If f × λ does not match the measured speed well, discuss measurement uncertainty rather than concluding the relationship is false; look at whether timing or wavelength readings are the larger source of error.

If a learner expects larger-amplitude waves to be faster, compare the measured speeds at different (small) amplitudes — they should be close within measurement error for the same medium, depth and frequency.
activities.intendedInsight: v = fλ can be discovered from measurement rather than taken on faith, and for small amplitudes changing the amplitude does not noticeably change the wave speed — speed depends on the medium and setup (e.g. water depth).
learnerActions: In a ripple tank (or equivalent setup), measure frequency and wavelength for several waves and compute f × λ.
Compare f × λ with an independently measured wave speed and note how closely they agree.
Change the amplitude of the waves and check whether the measured speed changes.
Write a one-sentence conclusion about the relationship f × λ represents and about whether amplitude affects speed.
activities.title: Measure the wave equation (empirical option)
